Redcare Pharmacy N.V. · RDC-DE · Investment memo

Redcare: Europe's online pharmacy leader turns profitable in FY27, and the return on offer comes from delivering what is already forecast, bought at a price that discounts doubt

Written 10 November 2026 for Richard. The model prices the shares at €77.90 (23 October 2026); the shares closed at €74.30 on 29 October, the day of the Q3 results. Bases, sources and open items are in the end-notes.

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The bottom line for Richard

Redcare is a bet on delivery, not on beating forecasts. Our forecasts equal consensus at EBITDA, the shares trade at about a fair multiple, and the return of about +40% to +70% to end-2027 comes entirely from earnings arriving.

  • Now to March 2027: EBITDA estimates are more likely to fall than to rise, and the first FY27 margin guide (3 March 2027) is more likely to disappoint than to impress.
  • From May 2027: the skew turns positive if Q1 2027 shows a clean Sevenum go-live and contained co-payment cover. A dated run of confirmations then follows.
  • The risk is one of size, not of direction or survival: a fair trough is 30-40% below the share price.

The business. Redcare is Europe's largest online pharmacy. About 40% of its revenue is prescription medicine (German and Swiss) and about 60% is non-prescription. The value sits in one revenue stream: German prescriptions. In that stream the state fixes the price and pays the pharmacy a fee per pack. Nearly every German prescription is now electronic, yet only 1-2% are filled online, and Redcare fills about two thirds of those. Redcare's German prescription revenue is growing at more than 50% a year through a logistics network that is already built.

The case. FY27 should be the first profitable year in Redcare's 25-year history and its first year of positive free cash flow. The model has EPS of €2.20 in FY27, €3.45 in FY28 and €4.36 in FY29, on an EBITDA margin rising from 2.9% in FY26 to 4.45% in FY29. The direction of Redcare's earnings is unusually well founded: about three quarters of the improvement rests on things already shown or already written into law. The size of Redcare's earnings is geared and narrowly based: EPS is a claim on roughly one and a half points of margin above close-to-fixed charges, and that margin turns on three nodes (the patient give-back, the Sevenum automation and the state), each of which has caused a miss before.

Where the risk/reward is skewed to the positive, and where it is not.

So the return on offer is the return to delivering what is already forecast, bought at a valuation that discounts doubt. It is not the return to beating forecasts.

The five judgements that move the value most (the arithmetic is in #9):

  1. How much Redcare and DocMorris hand back to patients after co-payments rise on 1 January 2027.
  2. Whether the Sevenum automation goes live cleanly in Q1 2027, and whether its first year saves €8m or €20m.
  3. Whether the state leaves the fee per pack and the co-payment waiver alone.
  4. Whether German prescription revenue keeps its 2026 pace and the non-prescription half holds its growth.
  5. Whether the margin keeps rising in H2 2027, once the fee stops helping. The H2 2027 margin sets FY28 and FY29 earnings power.

The return. The model's return at the guideline fair multiple is +542% to end-2027. Nine tenths of that return is a re-rating to 114.81 times earnings, a multiple drawn from years in which earnings were close to zero. My fair multiple is 25 to 30 times two-year forward earnings, which gives about +40% to +70% over the same 14 months, all of it from earnings arriving. A fair trough is 30-40% below the share price.

#1Strong or improving tailwinds in the operating environment; an absence of headwinds and risks

Conclusion on #1: The tailwinds are strong, dated and accelerating in volume, but the fee's help per pack ends in mid-2027, and headwinds are not absent: the headwinds are political and competitive, unlikely to land within 18 months and large if they do.

Evidence.

  • The shift of prescriptions online is accelerating, and the shift lifts the whole online channel, not one company. German statutory prescriptions form a market of about €55bn growing about 4% a year. Redcare's German prescription revenue grew 55%, 58% and 56% in the first three quarters of 2026; DocMorris' German prescription growth accelerated to 78% in Q3. Redcare added 123,000 prescription customers in Q3, twice Q2's number, which answers the earlier worry that customer acquisition had stalled.
  • The regulatory supports carry dates. The fee per pack rose from €8.35 to €9.00 in July 2026 and rises to €9.50 in January 2027. Since July 2026, repeat prescriptions for stable chronic patients can cover six months. The app-based redemption route (CardLink) is licensed to 31 March 2028. In July 2025 the Federal Court of Justice confirmed that EU mail-order pharmacies may pay prescription bonuses, which German pharmacies may not.
  • Patient co-payments rise 50% on 1 January 2027: the minimum from €5 to €7.50 and the maximum from €10 to €15. Only EU mail-order pharmacies may waive co-payments. One trade-press report says the co-payment regulation still awaits the Bundesrat (the upper house of parliament); that report should be checked.
  • The headwinds sit in the non-prescription 60% of revenue and in politics. Non-prescription growth was 9.4% in Q3 against guidance of 10-12%, and October began below 10%. A Bundestag member from the Christian Social Union (CSU) has asked the health ministry to ban co-payment waivers by EU mail-order pharmacies through the pending digital health act; the pharmacists' association has supplied the wording, and the current draft of the act does not contain the ban. The Health Finance Commission's €42.3bn savings agenda for 2027 has not become a bill that touches pharmacy pay, and no broker has analysed the chance that it will.

Inference. Three conclusions follow that a plain list of tailwinds hides.

  1. The fee tailwind is nearly spent. Net of the higher rebate to insurers and the signature rule, the January 2027 fee step is worth about €0.10 a pack more than H2 2026. Of the roughly €7m that the fee adds in FY27, about €6m is the July 2026 step running through the first half of 2027. From Q3 2027 the fee gives almost no help.
  2. The co-payment rise is a cost first and a benefit second. The co-payment rise makes the waiver worth €2.50 to €5 more a pack to the patient, which pulls patients online. The same rise makes the waiver promise 50% dearer for Redcare to keep, and far more visible to politicians: the state raised co-payments to fund the insurers, and the mail-order pharmacies are absorbing the rise on their patients' behalf.
  3. Redcare's success carries its own brake. Pressure from pharmacists and insurers grows with the online share. The volume tailwind and the political risk are one force seen from two sides.

So what. For the next 12 to 24 months the operating environment adds volume with high confidence, and adds little further profit per pack after mid-2027. Redcare's prescription engine is safe from competitors' prices and exposed to the state's pen.

The strongest counter-case is the 2021 precedent. A ban on prescription bonuses took effect in December 2020. Redcare's German prescription sales fell 34.6% in 2021, guidance was cut that July, and the sector de-rated by about 70% over two years. Today's differences are real: e-prescription rails now exist, so convenience no longer depends on a bonus, and two court rulings stand in the way of a ban. But a ban written into social law is a new route around those rulings. A separate proposal, that insurers collect co-payments directly, would remove the waiver without any ban; insurers resist that proposal for its administrative cost.

What would change my view. Negatively: a version of the digital health act that contains the waiver ban, a ministry statement adopting the ban, or any bill that raises the rebate. Positively: the annual fee review due from 2028 producing indexation (2-3% a year would add €4-6m a year, which is in nobody's forecasts), or prescription customer additions holding above 100,000 a quarter.

Against the market. I agree with the sell-side on the direction and size of the channel shift. I differ on three connections that the sell-side does not make: it counts the January fee step and the co-payment rise as plain tailwinds, and it dismisses the politics ("lots of noise, little substance"). I put the chance of a restriction on bonuses or waivers at 15-20% within three years, at 5% or less for a restriction in force within 18 months, and at about one in three for a draft or statement that moves the shares before then.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. The external force is structural, dated and in part enacted: German e-prescriptions are almost fully electronic but only 1-2% are filled online, Redcare's German prescription revenue grew 55-58% a quarter in 2026 with DocMorris accelerating to 78%, and the fee step (July 2026, January 2027), six-month repeat scripts, CardLink to 2028 and the court ruling on bonuses are already in force. Consensus sales growth at the 86th percentile fits, but the force reaches the 40% prescription half, not the soft non-prescription 60% (9.4% against 10-12% guided), the per-pack fee help ends by mid-2027, and the co-payment rise invites a give-back contest with DocMorris and a low-probability political threat to the waiver. That is a strong leg that reaches only part of sales and is trimmed by fading price and a direct threat, so it sits at the 75 level, just under the group's 80, below Arteche and above RELX.

#2Strong or improving internally-driven corporate change forces; an absence of problems and risks

Conclusion on #2: Corporate change is strong, funded and pointed at profit and cash. The problems are concentrated in people and in the one thing Redcare has never achieved: holding a margin gain for more than a year.

Evidence.

  • The owners changed the leadership team on purpose. The founder-chair, who holds 8.3%, replaced a pharmacy operator with a marketplace chief executive (in post since 1 October 2026) and an Amazon-trained finance director (in post since December 2025). The commercial director's post has been vacant since April 2026.
  • The plan moved from buying growth to harvesting it. Marketing fell from above 7% of revenue to about 5%. Management's message moved to EPS and cash. Positive free cash flow in FY27 is now a formal target.
  • The capital cycle is ending. The €100m automation of the Sevenum hub, Redcare's main warehouse, is installed and in testing, with go-live in Q1 2027. The automation doubles capacity and is designed to cut labour cost per order by 70%. Capital spending falls from about 4% of revenue in FY25 to below 2% from FY27, and no further capacity is needed for five years.
  • The new chief executive's first public statement was the helpful one: execution and monetisation, no strategic reset, and a marketplace and retail media business "in their infancy" to be scaled slowly.
  • Three things went the wrong way this autumn. International slipped back into loss (a margin of −0.4% in Q3 after +0.9% in Q2). Retail media grew more slowly than revenue. And Redcare raised its prescription bonus for new customers to answer DocMorris. A fourth item is new and neutral: a €40m secured loan from Deutsche Bank for Sevenum, with the rate and maturity undisclosed.

Inference. Redcare does not have to prove that it can reach the margin level; it has to prove that it can keep it. Redcare reached a 3% margin in FY23 and gave the gain back within a year by choice, through promotions in late 2024 and again in Q4 2025. What differs now is structural: a higher fee, a larger base of repeat orders, and an owner-led board that has made cash the objective. Whether management's behaviour differs will show first in Q4 2026, the promotional quarter, for which guidance leaves room for a margin anywhere from 1.4% to 3.4%.

So what. The gross drivers of the EBITDA increase from FY26 to FY28 sum to about €105m before cost inflation and give-backs, and about €80m of that sum rests on what is already shown or enacted. The parts still to be shown are Sevenum (€18m by FY28), monetisation (about €9m) and an International segment that must improve by about €9m. The thesis does not need the two capabilities Redcare most visibly lacks: retail media at scale and an owned telemedicine funnel.

The strongest counter-case is a thin leadership bench under a heavy load. A chief executive with no pharmacy experience meets a logistics go-live, a co-payment contest and a political initiative in the same five months. The chief operating officer, a pharmacist with more than ten years on the board, is the bridge between the new chief executive and the operation. Her departure would matter.

What would change my view. Negatively: a Q4 2026 margin below 2.5%, a Sevenum go-live that slips out of Q1 2027, or a further senior departure. Positively: a commercial director of calibre, or an overhead programme of the kind DocMorris has announced. A Redcare overhead programme could plausibly be worth €15-25m a year and is in nobody's numbers, including ours.

Against the market. The market sold the leadership change (the shares fell 15% in a day) and then accepted it; the sell-side calls the change "evolution, not reset". I agree, and I think the risk of a reinvestment year has fallen since the Q3 call. I differ on Sevenum's first year. Management and the brokers quote about 50bp of margin in 2027. Our forecasts take €8m, about 20bp, because logistics start-ups in this industry have been slow and costly in their first year: Redcare's own in 2021, Apotea's hub and Meds' warehouse move.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. The owners have made a deliberate, funded turn from buying growth to harvesting it: a new marketplace chief executive and Amazon-trained finance director, marketing cut from above 7% to about 5% of sales, the €100m Sevenum automation installed and going live in Q1 2027 (designed to cut labour per order by 70%, worth €8-22m a year), capital spending halving and positive free cash flow a formal FY27 target, with Q2 and Q3 margins up about 100bp. Held back by what is not yet shown and by present problems: a chief executive three weeks in post with no pharmacy experience, a vacant commercial director, International back in loss, retail media lagging, a raised prescription bonus, and a company that has never held a margin gain beyond a year; so it matches the group's 70, just below Theon and above OEM International.

#3Value chain and industry structure; competitive advantage and barriers; financial profile; management, strategy and culture

Conclusion on #3: The industry structure and Redcare's place in it are top-tier. Redcare's business model has scale and legal advantages but no pricing power. Redcare's financial profile is below average in level and well above average at the margin. Management is credible in finance and unproven at the top.

Evidence.

  • Structure. Prescription prices are fixed, so nobody competes on the price of the product. The incumbents are about 16,600 pharmacies that the law forbids from forming chains and from paying bonuses. Online, two companies hold about 80% of prescriptions: Redcare has about 67% of app redemptions and roughly twice DocMorris' German prescription sales. The tail of smaller online pharmacies is failing (two insolvencies in 2026), and the entrants the market feared (dm, Amazon) have made no dent.
  • Advantage. Scale gives Redcare the lowest cost per order and the cheapest customer acquisition. The law gives EU mail-order pharmacies a right that the incumbents lack. Chronic patients reorder: 90% of orders are repeat orders, and prescription customers give the service a net promoter score of about 80. There is no network effect and no pricing power: the state sets the prescription price, and Redcare chooses to price non-prescription products below rivals.
  • Financial profile. Weak in level: margins of 2-3%, operating losses in every year from FY19 to FY25, and a negative return on capital. Strong at the margin: the network is built, an extra euro of either prescription or non-prescription revenue brings about 9-10 cents of contribution, and capital spending is falling. The balance sheet is comfortable. The only material instrument is a €300m convertible bond due 2032 with a 1.75% cash coupon and a conversion price of €173.74, which holders can put back to Redcare in April 2030 for about €321m.
  • Management and culture. The finance director has rebuilt credibility. The chief executive is unproven at Redcare. Governance is clean: one share class, long-term-only pay, and no insider selling in a year. The goals stretch: a 5% margin within three years of March 2026, and above 8% in the long term. A service culture shows in the customer numbers; it does not show on the warehouse floor, where staff turnover is 39%.

Inference. Redcare is a medium-quality business inside a high-quality structure. Two points sharpen that judgement.

  1. The moat protects the duopoly against the incumbents, not Redcare against DocMorris. The legal right and the e-prescription rails are shared. DocMorris is recapitalised, at break-even, and owns the telemedicine funnel (TeleClinic) that Redcare lacks.
  2. Redcare's core business already earns the forecast margin. The DACH segment's margin was 4.2% in Q3 2026, above the 4.0% the whole group is forecast to earn in FY28. The forecast needs the core to hold slightly above today's margin through the co-payment contest, and the periphery to stop losing money. For the core, that is a low bar.

So what. The structure makes the volume forecast robust, and makes share loss to a third party unlikely within three years. The structure does not protect the margin, because the two leaders compete through what they give patients, and it does not protect Redcare against the state.

The strongest counter-case on the financial profile is that Redcare's low margin is only immaturity. Apotea runs the same model at a 4-6% operating margin. I think part of the gap is structural. Swiss specialty prescriptions earn almost nothing, German non-prescription pricing is fought on comparison sites, and Redcare shares its scale with customers by design. Those three reasons are why 5%, not 8%, is the realistic ceiling inside the forecast period.

What would change my view. Negatively: a third scaled competitor in prescriptions, or evidence that DocMorris has closed the gap in cost per order. Positively: disclosure of cohort retention that proves the repeat base.

Against the market. The market pays more per euro of sales for DocMorris (0.65 times FY27 sales against 0.45 times for Redcare), which says the market pays for the rate of change, not for position. On structure and position, I think the leader deserves the premium. On evidence of a rising margin, the market is right to wait.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. Qualitatively the structure is top-tier (leader with about two thirds of online prescription redemptions in a two-company channel, state-fixed prices, 16,600 incumbents barred from chains and bonuses, 90% repeat orders, a net promoter score of about 80), but the advantage is scale and a legal right shared with DocMorris and redrawable by the state, with no pricing power and no network effect, and management is credible in finance but unproven at the top. The financial profile is bottom-decile in level (return on invested capital −5%, 5th percentile; EBITDA margin 1.6%, 3rd percentile; losses FY19-FY25; margin swinging up to three points a year) though better at the margin (9-10 cents of contribution per extra euro, Sevenum's capital earning a decent return), so it is a leading position in a structure that caps margins, coherent with the groups (76, 62, 32, 50), between Vodafone and Munters.

#4Conservative guidance; proactivity in keeping expectations conservative; record of delivery and of raising guidance and estimates

Conclusion on #4: Guidance is deliberately conservative and the recent record of raising guidance is good. But the conservatism and the raises sit in revenue, while the margin, which drives EPS, is guided at the outcome and has a history of disappointing.

Evidence. In March 2026 the new finance director reset expectations and then raised revenue guidance twice; he never touched the margin range, although Q2 and Q3 ran at 3.5% and 3.4%. Management also warned of an H2 slowdown in prescriptions that did not arrive.

The longer record is two-sided. Revenue guidance was met or beaten in 2022, 2023 and 2026. Margins disappointed whenever promotions ran hot or logistics moved: in 2021, late 2024 and Q4 2025.

Inference. Under this finance director, revenue guidance is a floor set about three and a half points below the outcome, and the top of the margin range is set at the outcome. The conservatism is real on revenue. On the margin the conservatism is thinner than it looks, because Q2 and Q3 are the seasonal peak quarters and Q4 and Q1 are the weak ones.

So what, with probabilities.

  • FY26. A further raise or beat of prescription guidance: 45%. The margin in the upper half of its range: 70%. Non-prescription growth at or just below the bottom of its range, with no consequence for the group.
  • The first FY27 guide, 3 March 2027. I expect revenue growth in the low double digits, German prescription revenue of €850-900m or more, and a margin range of about 3.0-3.5%. I put 55% on a margin midpoint below consensus (3.5%), 35% on a midpoint at consensus, and 10% on a midpoint above.
  • During 2027. Revenue or prescription guidance raised at least once: 55%. Margin guidance raised: 20%. Margin guidance cut: 17%.
  • The 5% margin target. Met on time: 15%. Reached late or quietly re-dated: 65%. Formally lowered: 15%. Raised: 5%.

The guidance pattern Richard looks for is present: conservative guidance, active management of expectations and ad hoc raises. The pattern's limit is that it produces upgrades to the line that carries the least EPS.

The strongest counter-case is that margin guidance is sandbagged more than I allow. The core already earns 4.2%, and management repeats a Sevenum benefit more than twice the one in our forecasts. If the counter-case is right, FY27 could be guided at 3.5% and delivered at 3.8% or more.

What would change my view. A Q4 2026 margin at or above 3.2% would say the conservatism is deeper than I think. A first FY27 margin range whose top is below 3.5% would say the co-payment contest is costing more than the base case.

Against the market. I agree with the market's reading of the pattern; consensus sits at the top of every FY26 range. I differ on 3 March 2027. The market treats the first FY27 guide as a routine step. I think 3 March is the date on which a small adverse share-price reaction is most likely without any change in fundamentals. The March 2026 precedent was severe because expectations were far above the guide; this time expectations are not.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. Since the March 2026 reset the finance director has guided revenue as a floor and raised it twice (to 16-18% and €730-760m of German prescriptions), but the reset itself was a large expectations cut (the mid-term margin target from 8% to 5%, FY27 EPS still 57% below a year ago), margins disappointed in late 2024 and Q4 2025, and the margin range is set at the outcome rather than below it. A short good record after a recent rebasing with misses inside the window places it near the middle, below the group's 62 because the misses and the reset fall inside two years, between CVS Group and Yara.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops: does revenue growth lead to outsized profit growth?

Conclusion on #5: Redcare has strong operating leverage, fading financial leverage, specific cost-out and reinforcing feedback loops, but no pricing power of its own. Profit growth is therefore outsized in both directions, and depends on the margin, not on revenue.

Evidence.

  • EPS is a claim on the margin above a fixed hurdle. In FY27 the charges below EBITDA (depreciation and net financial items) are close to fixed at about €83m. Those charges absorb a margin of 2.1% before a euro of profit is earned, against a forecast margin of 3.55%. On the reported-like basis the hurdle is 2.5%.
  • The gearing is therefore steep. Each 10bp of margin is about €3.9m of EBITDA and about €0.15 of EPS: 7% of EPS on the model basis and 10% on the reported-like basis. Each 1% of revenue is worth about €3.5m of EBITDA and €0.14 of EPS. In FY27, revenue up 13% becomes EBITDA up 39% and EPS up 190%.
  • 2026's margin gains were half one-off and mix. The margin rose about 100bp year on year in both Q2 and Q3. About 90bp of Q2's 210bp fall in the marketing ratio was a one-off cut in absolute marketing spending, and that cut is finished: in Q3 marketing spending was flat. Much of the rest of the gain mirrors the shift in mix. German prescriptions carry a gross margin of about 13-14%, against about 30% for non-prescription products. So each point of revenue that moves to prescriptions takes about 17bp off the gross margin, and gives most of that back through lower marketing and fulfilment cost per euro. Stripped of mix, the one-off cut, the fee and a swing in non-prescription pricing, the repeatable gain was about 90bp in Q2 and 40bp in Q3, at 18-20% revenue growth. At the 13% growth forecast, the repeatable gain is 40-45bp a year.
  • Pricing power belongs to the state, not to Redcare. The one price rise in the forecasts is the fee per pack.
  • Cost-out is specific. Sevenum is worth €8m in FY27, €18m in FY28 and €22m by FY29; some €9m of new depreciation absorbs about half of those savings below EBITDA. The marketing ratio drifts from 5.0% to about 4.6% as repeat orders build up.
  • Financial leverage is modest and fading. A 10% move in operating profit moves pre-tax profit by about 13% in FY27 and by 10-11% by FY30.

Inference. Revenue growth does lead to outsized profit growth at Redcare, and by a wide margin. But the amplifier is a thin margin over fixed charges, not pricing power, and the amplifier works identically in reverse.

The feedback loops are coupled. The reinforcing loops (repeat customers building up, volume running through fixed costs) are what make a 40-65bp annual margin rise forecastable. The balancing loops (the rival's response, the political response) engage sooner the faster prescriptions grow. The balancing loops cap the margin, and make the four-year range of outcomes for the margin (about 4-5.5% in FY30) narrower than the range for revenue.

So what. The margin is the variable to forecast, and the give-back to patients is the variable inside the margin. A 25bp change in marketing-plus-bonus spending is worth about three times a 1% revenue miss.

The strongest counter-case is the simple reading of 2026: an incremental margin of 8% in Q2, and hence a 5% margin by FY28 on mechanical levers alone, with EBITDA above €200m. The simple reading fails on its own arithmetic once mix is netted against marketing. Q3, with flat marketing spending and a 40bp repeatable gain, is the evidence.

What would change my view. H2 2027 is the clean test. A margin gain of 50bp or more year on year in H2 2027, with no help from the fee, would move me towards the company's path. A gain of 20bp or less would say that even 4.0% in FY28 is too high.

Against the market. The sell-side describes the 2026 margin gain as marketing efficiency plus a harmless mix effect, and Deutsche Bank thinks 5% in FY28 is achievable. I think the repeatable rate is about half of what 2026 suggests, and that a 5% margin arrives around FY30. On the existence and direction of the leverage, the sell-side and I agree.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. The structure is strongly geared: charges below EBITDA are close to fixed at about €83m (a 2.1% margin hurdle against a 3.55% forecast), each extra euro of revenue brings 9-10 cents of contribution, so 13% revenue growth becomes 39% EBITDA growth and EPS nearly tripling in FY27, with specific cost-out (Sevenum €8-22m) and a reinforcing repeat-order loop; the gearing has been shown in both directions in the margin's past swings. It is held below 75 because the gear is a thin margin over fixed charges rather than pricing power (the state sets prescription prices, Redcare undercuts on non-prescription), the repeatable margin gain is about 40-45bp a year rather than 2026's 100bp, financial leverage is modest and fading, and the rival's and state's responses cap the margin; between the groups' 32 and 72.

#6Forecast financials; scope for double-digit growth; scope for higher growth and margins than the past

Conclusion on #6: Double-digit revenue growth and much faster profit growth are well supported to FY29, and margins should exceed anything in Redcare's past. Our forecasts sit on consensus, so they are a base to be delivered and not a source of surprise.

The forecasts of record. Revenue, EBITDA, EPS and free cash flow all improve together for the first time in Redcare's history.

Against the tests in the question.

  • Double-digit growth: yes for revenue through FY29, and far more for profit. EBITDA compounds at about 27% a year from FY26 to FY30, and EPS grows 57%, 26% and 31% in FY28, FY29 and FY30, after the FY27 inflection.
  • Higher growth and margins than the past: margins yes, growth no. Revenue growth halves from about 25% a year in FY20-FY25. The margin moves from an average of about 1.5%, swinging by up to three points a year, to a steady rise.

Against consensus, our forecasts sit on the numbers at EBITDA; the large EPS gaps are basis and tax. Our revenue is 0.2%, 0.8% and 1.5% above consensus for FY26, FY27 and FY28. Our EBITDA is 1% above consensus for FY26 and FY27 and 4% below for FY28. The model summary shows our FY27 EPS 66% above consensus, but that gap is a difference of basis. Like for like (reported-like €1.55 against €1.32) the gap is 17%, and most of that gap is tax. We charge 18%, because €312m of unrecognised Dutch tax losses shelter half of profit above €1m; the brokers charge about 25%.

Three points on the figures themselves.

  1. FY26 will be a loss on the reported basis. The first profitable year the market will recognise is FY27.
  2. FY29 EPS growth is clipped by accounting. The forecasts assume that the Dutch tax losses are recognised at end-FY28. Recognition lifts the accounting tax rate from 18% to 26% with no change in cash tax, and produces a one-off credit of €60-70m in reported earnings only.
  3. Net debt is moderate and falls fast. On FactSet's definition, with leases and the convertible at book value, net debt is about €243m at end-FY26, about 2.4 times EBITDA, and falls below one times EBITDA by FY29. Two model items that need care (the share count and the net cash line) are in the end-notes.

I change no forecast input. I considered two changes and judge that neither clears the bar.

  • The report that DocMorris will cover co-payments in full argues for a higher cost of co-payment cover than the €6m in the FY27 base. Against that report, Sevenum is installed and testing well, and management's figure for Sevenum is about €11m above ours. The two roughly offset, and both resolve by May 2027.
  • The new €40m Deutsche Bank loan probably adds about €1m a year of net interest, about €0.04 of EPS. The loan's terms are undisclosed and the amount is inside the tolerance of the interest line.

The strongest counter-case to the shape of the forecast is that Redcare has never done what it describes: a margin that rises three years running. The margin history is −0.3%, 3.0%, 1.4%, 2.0%, then 2.9% expected for FY26. The precedents say such forecasts are met late: Apotea needed four years to regain a 5% margin after opening a new hub.

What would change the forecasts. Up: Sevenum delivering management's figure in its first two quarters, an overhead programme, or fee indexation from 2028. Down: the give-back gauge in #9 falling by more than 50bp in Q1 2027, a Sevenum quarter lost, or German prescription revenue rising by less than €10m from one quarter to the next (the base case needs €12-15m).

Against the market. There is no gap to speak of at EBITDA, and that absence is the point: the case is delivery, not surprise. Beyond FY27 our forecasts are below the company's target and below the higher brokers.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. Very high growth from an inflection off near-zero earnings gives C, but I place it in the upper part of the band because the growth is organic and mechanical (revenue 10-13% a year, EBITDA about 27% a year) and the margin path (2.9% to 4.85%) rises above anything in the company's past, with the forecasts on consensus EBITDA; held off the top of the band because the company has never raised its margin three years running and the FY27 EPS cone is roughly −45% to +30%.

#7Scope for forecasts to lead to upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over the coming 6-12 months

Conclusion on #7: The forecasts are likely to lead to revenue-led guidance raises and to a better investor narrative from mid-2027, but not to EBITDA upgrades over the next six months, when estimate momentum is more likely to fade than to build.

Guidance. Revenue and prescription guidance are likely to be raised again (the probabilities are in #4), most plausibly in June or July 2027, as in 2026. A raise to margin guidance is unlikely before the Q3 2027 report, for three reasons: this finance director has never raised margin guidance, Q1 is the weak quarter and carries the Sevenum go-live, and the fee's help ends at mid-year.

Sell-side estimates. I expect revenue estimates to be nudged up, FY27 EBITDA consensus to stay within 3% of today's €138m with the first move down, and the breadth of revisions to fade from strongly positive to neutral by early 2027.

  • Where FY27 EBITDA consensus ends against today's €138m: more than 3% higher, 25%; within 3%, 45%; more than 3% lower, 30%.
  • FY28 EBITDA consensus (€182m, a 4.2% margin): cut, 45%; held, 35%; raised, 20%.
  • Why the breadth of revisions fades. The big upgrades of April to September drop out of the measurement windows. The first estimate change after Q3 was down (Deutsche Bank cut its FY27 EPS from €2.04 to €1.98). Q4 gives no reason to raise margins. And the first FY27 guide is likely to sit below consensus.
  • EPS consensus is the wild card, for a dull reason. Brokers reach FY27 EPS of €0.84 to €2.04 from near-identical EBITDA, because they treat the amortisation of acquired intangibles, the stock option cost and the non-cash convertible interest differently. When Redcare starts guiding below EBITDA, which the finance director has signalled, the median EPS estimate can move 10-20% with no change in the business. Our tax view adds a real but uncertain €0.15-0.19 a share.

Real upside to the numbers would come from four sources. Sevenum at management's 50bp is the largest identifiable source: about €11m, or 8% of FY27 EBITDA. Next come a co-payment rise that pulls more patients online than forecast (prescription growth of +35% is worth about €6m), an overhead programme, and fee indexation from 2028.

The narrative is where the upgrade is. Analysts already describe a profitable compounder with regulated volume. Investors do not yet pay for one. The investors' doubts are the right ones: will a margin gain be kept, and will the state leave the bonus alone? The first doubt is answered on known dates:

  1. Early May 2027: Q1, the first margin under the new co-payment regime and with Sevenum live.
  2. Late July 2027: the first clearly profitable half on the reported basis, and the probable revenue guidance raise.
  3. October 2027 to March 2028: H2 2027, the proof that the margin rises without help from the fee; and positive free cash flow for the year, which I put at 60-65%.

So what for Richard's test. Over the next six months the probability of upgrades is not skewed to the positive: it is positive for revenue, and flat to slightly negative for EBITDA and for the breadth of revisions. Over months 6 to 12 the probability becomes positively skewed if, and only if, Q1 2027 is clean.

The strongest counter-case is that I am too cautious on the next six months. A strong winter season, a further prescription guidance raise before year-end (Jefferies expects one) and a restrained DocMorris on 12 November would keep revisions positive into the March guide.

What would change my view. DocMorris limiting co-payment cover to first orders or defined cohorts; a Q4 margin at or above Q3's; or a first FY27 guide with a margin midpoint at 3.5% or higher.

Against the market. The dashboard rates sell-side earnings momentum A, the best in its sector. I read that rating as a description of the last six months, not the next six. Against investors I am the more confident: I think the prescription profit stream is durable through 2027 and that FY27 will be profitable.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, splits: revenue and prescription guidance is more likely than not raised again (55% in 2027), but a revenue raise of a point or two is small against 13% growth, the first FY27 margin guide on 3 March is more likely below the 3.5% consensus (55%) than above it (10%), and a margin raise is only 20% likely against 17% for a cut. Consensus EBITDA is more likely cut than raised (FY27 30% against 25%, FY28 45% against 20%) after the first post-Q3 change was down, so the 98th-percentile six-month revisions are momentum, not scope; the narrative is the one part with real upside, conditional on a clean Q1 2027, which places it just under the group's 45-50 between Kerry and Carlsberg.

#8Current momentum in guidance, sell-side estimates, narrative and share price, and the same for key peers

Conclusion on #8: Momentum is currently strong in sell-side revisions and good but young in the share price. The stronger peer momentum is at DocMorris, and Redcare's estimate momentum is at or near its peak.

Evidence (dashboard ratings snapshot of 24 October 2026; revisions as at 25 October 2026).

  • Pinned dashboard ratings: sell-side earnings momentum A; technical momentum B; valuation A; thematic fit and momentum C.
  • Guidance: two raises in 2026, both of revenue.
  • Sell-side revisions to FY27 over one, three and six months: EPS +16%, +35% and +85%; EBITDA +4%, +8% and +14%; sales +1%, +2% and +4%; target prices +3%, +7% and +14%. Over twelve months FY27 EPS is still 57% lower and EBITDA 23% lower. Six of nine brokers rate the shares Buy or Overweight (67%). The median target price is €96.
  • Share price: +14.8% over three months and +62.6% over six, but −3.2% over twelve. The price is 35.8% above its 200-day average, and that average has risen in only one of the last twelve months. Relative strength is at the 86th percentile. The dashboard's Stage 2 bucket is "early".
  • Since those readings: the shares fell 6% on the Q3 results, on the implied Q4 and a soft October for non-prescription sales, and the first estimate change was a small cut.
  • Peers. DocMorris has the stronger momentum: guidance raised twice, break-even in Q3 ahead of plan, and shares up about 137% in 2026 to mid-October against 11% for Redcare. Within the dashboard's sector, Redcare's revision score (13) is the highest of eight. Apotea is rated B, C and C on technical momentum, earnings momentum and valuation; Galenica is rated D, C and C.

Inference. Momentum is strong in the sell-side's numbers, good but young in the share price, and absent on a twelve-month view. The upgrades were a recovery from a deep cut, not new highs. The price trend is one leg off a low, not an established uptrend. And Redcare's shares move on their own news: sector peers explain about 4% of daily moves. No sector move will cushion a stumble, and none will dilute a correct call.

So what. Momentum supports the case today and is close to its peak rate on estimates. The market regime is the one outside force that could move the multiple against good results: the regime is risk-off and hostile to loss-making, convertible-financed shares that have risen fast.

The strongest counter-case is that "early" is good. A stock one leg off its low, with the best revisions in its sector and a valuation rating of A, is where long uptrends begin.

What would change my view. A 200-day average that rises for three or four months running would confirm the trend. Monthly app-download data should be discounted: downloads fell 32% year on year in October, in the same period that prescription customer additions doubled.

Against the market. The market trades the monthly app-download tracker. I rank Redcare's reported customer additions and prescription revenue above the tracker, and would treat a tracker-driven fall in the shares as noise unless active users also fall.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Both measures in the top fifth with no part negative gives A: two revenue guidance raises in 2026, FY27 EPS revisions of +16%/+35%/+85% over one, three and six months (3-month revision at the 95.5th percentile, far above the revenue growth rate), 67% Buy ratings, the price 36% above its 200-day average, and peers (DocMorris) with even stronger momentum. Placed at the floor because the trend is young (the 200-day average has risen in only one of twelve months, the twelve-month return is −3%), the shares fell 6% on Q3 and the first estimate change since was a small cut, so estimate momentum is at or past its peak rate.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations

Conclusion on #9: The case is simple in its drivers and trackable in volume, but risky in size: EPS is a geared claim on one variable with three known failure points, all tested in the next five months, and with a low-probability, high-magnitude political tail behind them.

Simplicity. The case is simple to state and concentrated in its drivers. One variable, the margin, crossing a fixed layer of costs, produces the whole change in EPS and cash flow. The margin turns on three nodes and one mechanical stream:

  • the commercial give-back to patients (marketing, prescription bonuses, co-payment cover and non-prescription prices), which management decides quarter by quarter;
  • Sevenum, one logistics project;
  • the state, which sets the fee and can redraw the rules on bonuses;
  • and the mechanical stream of volume running through fixed costs, worth about 40-45bp of margin a year.

Each past miss came from one of the three nodes: the give-back in late 2024 and Q4 2025, logistics in 2021 and the state in 2021. All three nodes are on the calendar in the next five months. That is the most compact statement of the risk.

The range of outcomes for FY27 is mildly skewed to the bear in size and clearly skewed to the bear in speed. Revenue: plus or minus 3%. EBITDA: about €114m (bear), €139m (base) and €158m (bull), a margin of 3.0% to 3.9%. EPS: about €1.2 to €2.9. I weight the cases 25%, 55% and 20%, a shade more to the bear than the earlier work because of the report that DocMorris will cover co-payments in full; the weighted EBITDA is about €137m. Speed favours the bear: a co-payment contest or a commissioning problem shows within a quarter, while the favourable items accrue over several quarters.

The five judgements, and what a plausible error in each costs. In each calculation, FY27 depreciation and net financial items are held fixed, tax is 18% and the model divides by about 21.0m shares, so €10m of EBITDA is about €0.39 of EPS.

What each error does to the rest of the case.

1. The give-back after 1 January 2027

Base: targeted co-payment cover costing about €6m more than in 2026.
  • A further €2.50 on a quarter of Redcare's roughly 16m packs costs €10m, or 25bp of revenue: the margin falls from 3.55% to 3.3% and EBITDA from €139m to €129m.
  • Pre-tax profit falls from €56m to €46m, net income from €46m to €38m, and EPS from €2.20 to about €1.81 (−18%). Reported-like EPS falls from €1.55 to about €1.16 (−25%).
  • Free cash flow of about €10m on the model's definition falls to about €1m, which puts the positive free cash flow target on a knife edge.
  • A full contest (€20-40m) would leave EBITDA at €99-119m, no better than FY26, and EPS at €0.6-1.4. I put a full contest at about 20%.
  • Restraint (cover held to first orders) would add back about €6m, or €0.23 of EPS.

2. Sevenum's first year

Base: €8m of savings in FY27.
  • If management's 50bp is right, savings are €19.6m, or €11.6m more: EBITDA of €151m, a margin of 3.85%, and EPS up €0.45 to about €2.65.
  • If a quarter is lost (15-20% likely), up to €8m of cost and lost sales follow: EBITDA of €131m, a margin of 3.35%, and EPS down €0.31 to about €1.89.
  • Either way about €9m of new depreciation arrives; the forecasts already include it.

3. The state

Base: the fee, the rebate and the waiver stand.
  • Each €0.10 a pack across 16m packs is €1.6m of EBITDA, or €0.06 of EPS. A €0.50 adverse change in the rebate or fee is €8m, or €0.31 (14% of FY27 EPS), and would erase the whole FY27 fee gain.
  • Illustration: a waiver or bonus restriction biting in FY28. Prescription growth of 10% instead of 21% is €106m less revenue and about €10m less contribution; replacing the lost tool with 50bp more marketing costs about €21m; some bonus cost is saved. Net, €20-30m comes off FY28 EBITDA of €175m, leaving a margin of about 3.4-3.6% and EPS of €2.3-2.7 against €3.45. The multiple would fall too.

4. Volume

Base: prescriptions +27% in FY27, which needs only the 2026 pace of €12-15m more revenue each quarter; non-prescription +7-8%.
  • Prescriptions at +15%: €91m less revenue, €8.7m less EBITDA at about 9.5% contribution, and €0.34 less EPS.
  • Non-prescription and International three points slower: 3% of about €2.1bn is €62m of revenue, about €6m of EBITDA and €0.23 of EPS.
  • Prescriptions at +35%: €61m more revenue, about €6m of EBITDA and about €0.23 of EPS.
  • Volume errors are about a third the size of give-back errors. That ratio is why the case is predictable in direction and geared in size.

5. The self-propelled margin, from H2 2027

Base: 4.0% in FY28 and 4.45% in FY29; the evidence supports 3.6% to 4.6% for FY28.
  • FY28 at 3.6%: €17.5m less EBITDA, and EPS of €2.77 against €3.45 (−20%).
  • FY28 at 4.6%: €26m more EBITDA, and EPS of €4.47 (+30%).
  • FY29 is the year that the end-2027 share price will capitalise. Each 10bp of FY29 margin is €4.8m of EBITDA, €0.17 of EPS and, at 25 times, about €4 a share: 5% of today's price.

Tails outside the range, inside 18 months. A stumble when CardLink ends on 31 March 2028 and patients must move to the new identity-based redemption route: 5-10%. About 90% of redemptions run through the app, and the new route has real friction for patients over 55. A larger rebate to insurers from the savings agenda: 5-8%.

Trackability is good for volume and poor for the give-back. Volume is visible in prescription revenue and customer numbers each quarter, and in e-prescription counts each month. The give-back is not visible: bonus cost is deducted from revenue and never shown. The most useful gauge that can be built from disclosure is the gross margin less the marketing ratio, which nets out any shift of acquisition cost between the two lines. The gauge rose year on year in both Q2 and Q3 2026, so the total given back has so far fallen, not risen. A fall in the gauge of more than about 50bp year on year in Q1 2027 would say that the co-payment contest is costing more than the base case. The calendar is the constraint: there is no reported margin under the new co-payment regime until early May 2027.

Alarm: a fall of more than about 50bp year on year in Q1 2027.

Share-price risk is far wider than the fundamental range. The shares have moved 15% to 60% on single events: a drugstore chain's entry, the March 2026 reset and the chief executive's departure. A fair trough is about €45-55, 30-42% below the share price; that trough is roughly 9-10 times FY27 EBITDA, which is what a sceptical market pays for consensus without the runway. A fundamental break would take the shares to €30-35, where they stood in March 2026 and where Jefferies puts its downside case. Short interest is reported at about 17%, part of it hedging of the convertible; I could not verify the figure or its split.

The sector's precedents are about rules and logistics, not the economic cycle. Prescription revenue is reimbursed and not cyclical; the non-prescription half is mildly cyclical. The precedents are the 2021 bonus ban (#1), Apotea's margin falling four points in a year during a hub ramp-up and a price investment, and Zur Rose's decade of sub-scale losses and capital raises.

The strongest counter-case to a high-risk reading: the risks are dated, observable and largely priced by investors already; the balance sheet is funded to 2030; and the bear case for FY27 still has EBITDA 14% above FY26. Redcare's risk is one of size, not of survival or direction.

What would change my view. A clean Q1 2027, on both the gauge and Sevenum, removes two of the three nodes for the year and would halve the FY27 range of outcomes by July 2027.

Against the market. Jefferies' range of €35 to €120 around a €97 target shows that the sell-side knows the width. What the sell-side has not done is price the connections: no note models the cost of the co-payment contest or of the savings agenda. Investors, through the valuation discount and the short interest, price more risk than analysts describe. On the durability of the prescription profit through 2027, I think investors price too much risk.

Score: 24, set by the Rater. The memo's FY27 EPS range is about €1.2 to €2.9 around €2.20 (about −45% to +30%), because EPS is a geared claim on one margin that turns on three nodes (the patient give-back, the Sevenum go-live, the state's fee and waiver rules), each of which has caused a miss before and all of which are tested before May 2027, with the give-back untrackable in disclosure, a low-probability political binary behind it and a share price that has moved 15-60% on single events with short interest about 17%. Volume is trackable, demand non-cyclical and the balance sheet funded to 2030, which keeps it off the bottom; a range of a third or more either way on one geared variable places it at the 25 level, below the groups' 27 and 42 on the width of the cone, between Storskogen and TT Electronics.

#10Where the stock plausibly is in its lifecycle

Conclusion on #10: The stock is turning up, with the thesis starting to broaden from prescription volume to profit and cash. The stock earns the Reinforcing label only if Q1 and H1 2027 deliver.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places the stock in the Reinforcing phase, on the six-month price move and the revisions. The detail argues for an earlier stage:

  • The momentum in #8 is a first leg off a low, not an established trend.
  • Redcare has not yet reported a profitable year.
  • Estimates have recovered to where our independent work arrives, not beyond it.
  • The thesis has broadened among analysts, from "prescription volume" to "profit and cash". The thesis has not broadened among investors: the shares fell on a quarter in which prescriptions grew 56%.
  • The scope for upgrades is in revenue, not in the margin.

My placing: turning up, with the thesis beginning to broaden. The Reinforcing phase needs delivery that confirms the broader thesis and draws further upgrades. Neither has happened yet. The first chance is Q1 and H1 2027.

What moves the stock from here.

  • To reinforcing: a clean Q1 2027, a revenue guidance raise at mid-year, and a margin that rises in H2 2027 without help from the fee.
  • To stalling: a cut to FY27 margin guidance or a costly co-payment contest, either of which would revive the "margins never stick" reading.
  • To collapsing: a ban on co-payment waivers enacted.

So what. The lifecycle phase matters twice. The phase sets the multiple (#11): a turning-up stock earns the lower part of its range, because its forecasts are less certain. And the phase frames the opportunity: the most rewarding transition is ahead of Redcare, not behind it.

The strongest counter-case is that the dashboard's rule is right. A large six-month rise, two guidance raises and A-rated revisions are what the Reinforcing phase looks like, and if Q4 and DocMorris' Capital Markets Day are benign, the shares will not wait for May.

What would change my view. Two reported quarters of FY27 on plan would make the stock Reinforcing. A Q4 2026 margin below 2.5% would put the turning-up placing itself in question.

Against the market. The sell-side writes as if the thesis has already broadened. The share-price reaction to Q3 says investors have not granted the broader thesis.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's turning up with the thesis beginning to broaden rather than the computed Broadening or the dashboard's Reinforcing: the first profitable year is FY27, estimates have recovered to the independent forecast rather than beyond it, analysts have broadened the story to profit and cash but investors have not (the shares fell on a quarter of 56% prescription growth), and the most rewarding transition is ahead. It is held below the 75 level because the next six months look flat to down on EBITDA estimates with revision momentum near its peak and a toll gate at the March guide and Q1 2027, so it sits between Kuehne + Nagel and Tenaris.

#11The fair multiple

Conclusion on #11: The guideline fair multiple (114.81 times in the model, 154.88 times in the Phases file) is an artefact of a history with almost no earnings. My fair multiple is 25 to 30 times two-year forward earnings, with 35 times a ceiling once delivery is proven.

What the files give. The Phases file (9 November 2026) puts the stock in the Reinforcing phase and sets the guideline fair multiple at 154.88 times: the 90th percentile of the stock's ten-year history of the two-year forward P/E. The model summary applies 114.81 times, and the return in #12 is the model's, at 114.81 times. The multiple today is 30.1 times on consensus EPS and 26.6 times on the model's EPS. The ten-year range runs from 27.1 times at the 10th percentile to 64.8 times at the median and 102.5 times at the 75th percentile.

My view: the guideline multiple cannot be used for Redcare at this moment, at either figure. Four reasons support that view.

  1. The history measures the denominator, not what investors paid for earnings. Only 52 of 120 months have a multiple at all; in the other months, forward earnings were negative. In the months that do have a multiple, the multiple was struck on forecast earnings that never arrived: a share price of €130-200 on €1.2-1.6 of expected EPS in 2020-21, followed by losses. Investors valued the shares on sales and discounted cash flow, and the P/E was a by-product. A percentile of that P/E series says how thin expected profit was, not what a profitable Redcare is worth.
  2. When profits arrive, the multiple falls even if the shares rise. Zalando's forward P/E went from 316 times to 155 times to 102 times in its first three profitable years, while its EBITDA multiple went from 31 to 21 times. Apotea traded at about 41-43 times in its first two listed years and trades at about 23 times now. Chewy traded at 22.5 times EBITDA at first profit, and its sales multiple then nearly halved.
  3. The honest anchors are lower. Apotea trades at 23 times and Galenica at 20 times; Redcare's own multiple sits just above the dashboard's "crash" band; and the brokers' discounted cash flow targets are €97-104.
  4. My lifecycle phase is earlier than the dashboard's (#10), and the guideline's own logic gives a turning-up stock the lower part of its range.

My fair multiple: 25 to 30 times two-year forward EPS on the model basis for the next 12 to 18 months. That range is about where the stock trades today.

  • For a premium to Apotea and Galenica: EPS growing 25-55% a year off the inflection, a long runway, and a number-one position.
  • Against paying more: a state-granted profit, a 3-5% margin, and an EPS range of roughly −45% to +35% for FY27.
  • Ceiling: 35 times, once H2 2027 has proved the margin. A 35 times multiple is close to what closing the sales-multiple gap to DocMorris would imply (about €110 a share).
  • Trough: 18 to 20 times.
  • The same share price is about three multiple points higher on the reported-like EPS that brokers use.

So what. The case does not need a re-rating and should not count on one. The case needs the earnings to arrive.

The strongest counter-case is that first profits have earned 40 times or more for two years elsewhere (Apotea), and that a large short position could add fuel. At 40 times, the end-2027 value would be about €174 a share. I do not count on a 40 times multiple.

What would change my view. Delivery through H2 2027 would justify the top of my range and then the ceiling. A waiver ban would justify the trough.

Against the market. The guideline says 115 to 155 times. The market says 27 to 30 times. I side with the market on the level, and think the direction of the multiple from here is flat to modestly up, not a re-rating of four or five times.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. Cheap on one and neutral on the other would give B, but I move it to C because the cheap reading is an artefact: only 52 of 120 months have a multiple, struck on forecast earnings that never arrived, and a stock at its first profit and turning up deserves a lower multiple than that history, so on the memo's own fair multiple of 25-30 times the stock (26.6x model, 30.1x consensus) trades at about fair. Placed in the upper part of C because the sales-multiple discount to a smaller, less profitable rival and broker discounted cash flow values of €97-104 lean cheap.

#12Total shareholder return

Conclusion on #12: The model's +542% to end-2027 and +781% to mid-2029 are roughly nine tenths a re-rating that I do not expect. On a fair multiple of 25 to 30 times, the return is about +40% to +70% over 14 months and about +55% to +90% over three years, all from earnings growth and none from dividends.

The model's return at the guideline fair multiple.

  • To the 18-month column (31 December 2027): +541.9%, or +409.1% annualised; a value of €500.07 a share. From dividends, nil. From the multiple, +331.6% (26.6 to 114.81 times). From earnings, +48.8% (two-year forward EPS from €2.93 to €4.36, the FY29 figure).
  • To the three-year column (30 June 2029): +780.6%, or +127.9% annualised; €685.97 a share. From the multiple, +331.6%. From earnings, +104.0% (forward EPS to about €5.98).
  • The three parts multiply rather than add: 4.316 × 1.488 = 6.42 for the first horizon, and 4.316 × 2.040 = 8.81 for the second.

What drives the model's return.

  1. The multiple is nine tenths of the model's return. Hold the multiple at today's 26.6 times and the same model gives +48.8% to end-2027, about €116 a share.
  2. The earnings part is the real case. The earnings part comes from a margin rising about 155bp from FY26 to FY29 on revenue growing 10-13% a year, geared through fixed charges (#5). Of the EBITDA increase to FY30, about half is volume running through the network and about 40% is four discrete levers (Sevenum, the marketing-and-bonus ratio, monetisation and the fee), less about 30% for cost inflation, co-payment cover and reinvestment. Below EBITDA, finance cost drifts down, the tax rate steps up in FY29, and the share count grows 0.5% a year.
  3. Dividends and other cash returns are nil. Cash builds instead. The first call on that cash is the April 2030 put on the convertible. A buyback before 2030 is unlikely unless the shares approach the conversion price, where the bond becomes equity (8.4% more shares) and about €310m of debt disappears.

My reading, on the fair multiple from #11.

  • Next 6 to 18 months (to end-2027, about 14 months). FY29 EPS of €4.36 at 25 to 30 times is €109-131 a share: +40% to +68%. From earnings, +49%; from the multiple, −6% to +13%; from dividends, nil. At the trough multiple of 20 times the value is €87, +12%.
  • With earnings short. If the FY29 margin is 50bp lower, FY29 EPS is about €3.51. At 25 times that EPS is worth €88 (+13%); at 20 times, €70 (−10%). Delivered earnings make money even on a lower multiple. Losses come from earnings falling short, not from the multiple alone.
  • Three years (to mid-2029). Forward EPS of about €5.98 at 20 to 25 times is €120-149: +53% to +92%, or 17-28% a year. From earnings, +104%; from the multiple, −25% to −6%. I use a lower multiple for the three-year view because EPS growth slows towards 30%.
  • From the post-results price of €74.30, the 14-month range is +47% to +76%.
  • If the Phases file's 154.88 times were applied instead, the end-2027 value would be about €675. Neither guideline figure should be quoted as an expectation.

So what. The return is earnings growth and nothing else. The return is therefore exposed in full to the five judgements in #9, and to the basis on which the market chooses to capitalise EPS.

The strongest counter-case is the one in #11: a first-profit multiple of 40 times, which would roughly double the share price by end-2027.

What would change my view. The H2 2027 margin. The H2 2027 margin fixes FY28 and FY29 earnings power, and with it both the earnings part and the multiple part of the return.

Against the market. The brokers' median target of €96 is +23% over twelve months. My range is consistent with those targets rolled forward a year on delivered earnings, and far from the model's.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. The memo's base case of FY29 EPS of €4.36 at 25-30 times gives +40% to +68% to end-2027, all from earnings, and weighting about a quarter on a missed margin or a failed node (+13% to −10% at 20-25 times, a fair trough 30-40% below the price) leaves about +35-40%, with the three-year check of +53% to +92% supportive; that sits at the A threshold. I hold it at the floor of the band for the fat, sudden lower tail, since the return rests entirely on a geared margin arriving.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Redcare leads a structure that is close to ideal for a scaled online pharmacy. Prices are fixed, the state sets a fee per pack, the law keeps the fragmented incumbents small, and the online channel has two companies. Redcare's prescription volume is compounding at more than 50%, the network to carry that volume is built, and the capital cycle is ending. Those facts make the direction of earnings unusually well founded. FY27 should be the first profitable year and the first with positive free cash flow.

The size of earnings is another matter. EPS is a geared claim on one variable, the margin, which turns on what management gives back to patients, on one logistics project and on the state. Each of those three has caused a miss before, and all three are tested between now and May 2027. Our forecasts sit on consensus, so there is no cushion of expected upgrades at EBITDA: the upgrades on offer are to revenue guidance and, later, to the narrative.

The opportunity is therefore specific. The market is not being asked to believe more than the analysts already forecast; the market is being asked to believe that the forecast will be delivered, and it has priced that doubt into a low multiple of sales and a discount to the rival. If Q1 2027 shows a clean Sevenum go-live and contained co-payment cover, a dated sequence follows: a profitable first half, a probable revenue guidance raise, positive free cash flow, and an H2 margin that rises on its own. On a fair multiple, delivered earnings are worth about +40% to +70% by end-2027. If a node fails, the fair trough is 30-40% below the share price.

The most useful near-term evidence will not come from Redcare. It will come from what DocMorris says on 12 November about covering the higher co-payment, and from what the ministry does with the waiver proposal.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 78, set by the Rater. Strong external forces (an accelerating, dated channel shift of a €55bn prescription market online, at 77) and a funded internal turn to profit and cash (Sevenum, lower marketing and capex, at 70) are turning into a step-up in profits that is top-decile in the Universe (consensus EPS growth next year at the 99th percentile, EBITDA about +27% a year, the first profitable year in FY27). It falls short of Arteche's 80 and the 90 level because the forces reach the prescription 40% rather than the whole business, the per-pack fee help fades from mid-2027, and how surely the volume reaches profit depends on a give-back and a margin the company has never held.

Foundations' Robustness: 52, set by the Rater. An excellent, legally protected structure (leader of a two-company online channel taking a state-priced, non-discretionary pool from fragmented incumbents, with a 90% repeat-order base) is offset by a bottom-decile financial profile with margins that have swung by up to three points a year, no pricing power, a moat the state can redraw and a rival that shares it, an unproven chief executive, and a delivery record that is good on revenue but has a reset and margin misses inside two years. It lacks the top-decile stability that lifted CVS Group to 80, so it sits about typical, coherent with Quality at 52 and Guidance and delivery at 53.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 72, set by the Rater. The case fits Demand-driven EPS Upgrader in substance: a dated demand step-up in German online prescriptions (>50% growth), the capacity already built (the network, Sevenum installed) and a funded plan to convert volume into EPS, with a Major Cause-for-Concern Clearing element. It is held below 75 because the EPS step-up runs through margin gearing that has never held for long rather than through demand alone, and current problems (the co-payment give-back contest, International back in loss, a new chief executive) blur the mechanism until Q1 2027; that consensus already holds the step-up does not count here.

Case Riskiness: 26, set by the Rater. Riskiness and simplicity at 24 sets it: the case is simple to state but EPS is a geared claim on one margin with three known failure points all tested within five months, an FY27 EPS range of about −45% to +30%, a political binary behind it and a share price that has moved 15-60% on single events. It sits a little above Judges Scientific's 20 because demand is non-cyclical and trackable in volume, the multiple is at fair rather than high, and the balance sheet is funded to 2030, so the risk is one of size rather than survival.

End-notes: bases, sources and open items

Bases used throughout

  • Share price. The model and all returns use €77.90 (23 October 2026). The shares closed at €74.30 on 29 October 2026, the day of the Q3 results.
  • Forecasts. All forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model of record (model update 2).
  • EBITDA is the company's adjusted figure, which is also the figure the brokers use.
  • EPS is on the model basis (before the amortisation of acquired intangibles and the stock option cost) unless marked "reported-like", which is the basis most brokers submit. The same share price is about three multiple points higher on reported-like EPS.
  • Probabilities are the Analyst's judgement.
  • Abbreviations. DACH: Germany, Austria and Switzerland. CSU: Christian Social Union. EV: enterprise value. bp: basis points.

Open items in the model

  • Share count. The model appears to divide by about 21.0m shares against 20.6m in issue, which understates EPS by about 2%. The note to the Financial Analyst on the share count is still open.
  • Net cash line. The model's net cash line (−€99m at end-FY26) does not reconcile with its starting point. FactSet's net debt of about €243m (#6) is the figure used in the text.
  • Free cash flow definition. The model treats the non-cash part of the convertible's interest as cash, so Redcare will hold €8-20m a year more than the model's free cash flow.
  • Guideline multiple. The Phases file (154.88 times) and the model summary (114.81 times) do not agree, and the Financial Analyst should reconcile them. The returns in #12 use the model's 114.81 times.
  • FY29 consensus is only two brokers, at a 5.2% margin, and should not be used.

Points to verify

  • The trade-press report that the co-payment regulation still awaits the Bundesrat (#1).
  • The reported short interest of about 17% and its split between outright shorts and hedging of the convertible (#9).
  • In #2, the parts still to be shown (Sevenum €18m, monetisation about €9m, International about €9m) and the part already shown or enacted (about €80m) sum to more than the €105m gross total; the Analyst should confirm how the parts overlap.

Notes on the visuals

  • The guidance table in #4 shows the 15 June and 28 September raises together, because the memo does not say which step each raise took.
  • In the margin chart in #6, the history sequence (−0.3%, 3.0%, 1.4%, 2.0%) is the memo's; the fiscal-year labels FY22 to FY25 are the Visual Editor's reading.
  • In the summary timeline, the first six dates come from the summary of the Analyst's memo; the last three are drawn from #7 and #9.

Visuals: default charts and tables from model update 2 (default_visuals.py v0.8.2); further charts drawn by the Visual Editor and the Copy Editor from the memo's figures with chartkit. Probabilities are the Analyst's judgement.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
